## Why This Is Asked
This question assesses the ability to design a namespace-scoped canary workflow using standard CKAD primitives: CronJob, ConfigMaps, and Deployment rolling updates. It also tests observability knowledge via PVC-backed logs, status tracking patterns, and security awareness through NetworkPolicy and InitContainer usage.

## Key Concepts
- **ConfigMaps**: canary-config holds dynamic parameters (targetImage, canaryPercent); canary-status records rollout history and last-promotion timestamps
- **CronJob**: Provides periodic reconciliation that checks configuration and triggers conditional updates
- **Deployment RollingUpdate**: maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 ensures controlled, non-disruptive updates
- **Traffic Shifting**: Routes a configurable percentage of traffic to canary pods for gradual exposure
- **InitContainer**: Ensures jq availability for JSON parsing within the job
- **Probes**: Readiness gates ensure traffic only reaches healthy pods; liveness checks restart unhealthy instances
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricts namespace egress to approved registries only
- **PVC**: Persists job logs for debugging and audit trails

## Trade-offs
- **Pros**: Fully Kubernetes-native with no external dependencies; ConfigMap history provides auditability; automatic promotion reduces manual intervention
- **Cons**: Namespace-scoped only; NetworkPolicy requires CNI support; jq dependency increases image size; ConfigMaps lack built-in validation

## Why This Is Asked

This question tests practical RBAC auditing skills within the CKAD scope, including multi-namespace governance, secure logging, and egress constraints.

## Key Concepts

- **RBAC objects**: RoleBindings, ClusterRoleBindings, and ServiceAccounts at the namespace level
- **ConfigMap-driven policy**: External policy reference for audit rules
- **Namespace-scoped auditing**: Decentralized audit model vs. cluster-wide approaches
- **Pod lifecycle**: InitContainers for tool installation, readiness/liveness probes for reliability
- **Storage**: PVC-backed logging at /logs
- **Network security**: Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress to the audit endpoint

## Trade-offs

- **Pros**: Decentralized scaling, namespace isolation, ConfigMap flexibility for policy updates
- **Cons**: Resource overhead per namespace, potential for policy drift, Secret management complexity, duplicated effort across namespaces

## Minimal YAML Skeleton

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: rbac-policy
data:
  policy.yaml: |-
    allowedBindings:
      - kind: User
        name: admin
    maxServiceAccounts: 10
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: audit-credentials
type: Opaque
stringData:
  bearer-token: <token>
  endpoint: https://audit.example.com/api/v1/digest
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: audit-logs
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: rbac-auditor
  namespace: target-ns
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rbac-auditor
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: rbac-auditor
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: busybox
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - "wget -qO /tools/curl https://curl.se/download && wget -qO /tools/jq https://github.com/jqlang/jq/releases/download/jq-1.7.1/jq-linux64 && chmod +x /tools/*"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /tools
      containers:
        - name: auditor
          image: alpine:latest
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              apk add --no-cache curl jq
              while true; do
                kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings,serviceaccounts -o json > /logs/snapshot.json
                curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d @/logs/snapshot.json $ENDPOINT
                sleep 3600
              done
          env:
            - name: TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: audit-credentials
                  key: bearer-token
            - name: ENDPOINT
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: audit-credentials
                  key: endpoint
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: audit-logs
        - name: tools
          emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: audit-egress-restrict
  namespace: target-ns
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rbac-auditor
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: audit-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills around in-cluster tooling, Pod security checks, and non-intrusive governance in a namespace-scoped pattern. It avoids admission webhooks and reinforces RBAC, Secrets, PVCs, InitContainers, and NetworkPolicies.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped Deployment pattern without admission controllers
- SecurityContext defaults: non-root, readOnlyRootFilesystem, runAsUser
- Secret-backed Bearer token for API calls and in-cluster service accounts
- Logs persisted to a PVC; InitContainer for curl/jq
- Readiness/Liveness probes and a strict egress policy via NetworkPolicy

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: compliance-guard
  namespace: your-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: compliance-guard
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: compliance-guard
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: init-tools
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq > /dev/null 2>&1 || true"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
      containers:
        - name: guard
          image: your-registry/compliance-guard:latest
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: compliance-token
          env:
            - name: PORTAL_URL
              value: "http://compliance-portal:8080"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do ./guard --check-pod-security; sleep 60; done"]
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 1000
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
        
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-pvc
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          spreadConstraintLabelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: compliance-guard
```

- How would you scale this across thousands of namespaces?

## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates CKAD proficiency in extending namespace-centric validation using core Kubernetes primitives: ConfigMaps, Secrets, CronJobs, InitContainers, PVCs, and NetworkPolicies. It also tests knowledge of jq for in-cluster JSON Schema validation and idempotent status updates.

## Key Concepts

- **Namespace-scoped configuration**: All resources operate within a single namespace boundary
- **CronJob with InitContainer tooling**: InitContainer prepares the environment (curl/jq) before the main validation container runs
- **JSON Schema validation using jq**: jq processes ConfigMap data against the fetched schema
- **PVC-backed logging**: Persistent storage preserves logs across job executions
- **NetworkPolicy egress control**: Restricts outbound traffic to only approved endpoints
- **Status persistence in ConfigMap**: Validation results are stored for auditing and downstream consumption

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: ns-config-schema-validator
  namespace: <target-namespace>
spec:
  schedule: "*/7 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: busybox
            command: ["sh", "-c", "wget -O /usr/local/bin/jq https://github.com/jqlang/jq/releases/download/jq-1.7/jq-linux64 && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/jq"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /usr/local/bin
          containers:
          - name: validator
            image: curlimages/curl:latest
            env:
            - name: API_KEY
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: validation-creds
                  key: api-key
            command: ["sh", "-c"]
            args:
            - |
              SCHEMA_URL=$(kubectl get configmap validation-config -o jsonpath='{.data.schema-url}')
              curl -s $SCHEMA_URL -o /logs/schema.json
              for cm in $(kubectl get configmaps -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
                kubectl get configmap $cm -o json | jq -s ".[0] * {data: .[1] | getpath($cm | split(\"-\")[1:] | map(.))}" /logs/schema.json > /logs/validation-$cm.json || true
              done
              curl -X POST http://validation-portal:8080/api/v1/validate -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" --data-binary @/logs/summary.json
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /usr/local/bin
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: validation-logs
          - name: tools
            emptyDir: {}
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Trade-offs

| Aspect | Trade-off |
|--------|-----------|
| **InitContainer vs. Custom Image** | InitContainer adds startup latency but keeps the main image lightweight and avoids maintenance of a custom image. |
| **jq Validation vs. Dedicated Validator** | jq is lightweight and universally available, but lacks full JSON Schema draft support. A dedicated validator (e.g., kubeconform) offers better accuracy at the cost of added complexity. |
| **PVC for Logs** | Provides durability and debugging capability but introduces storage overhead and potential bottlenecks in high-frequency runs. |
| **NetworkPolicy Egress** | Restricts access to only required endpoints, enhancing security but requires careful planning of all dependencies. |
| **ConfigMap Status vs. Custom Resource** | ConfigMap is simpler and requires no CRD management, but lacks built-in versioning and conflict resolution. |
